title: Values Appearing Twice Sum
description: `nums` has length `n` and every value lies in `[1, n]`; each value occurs at most twice. Return the sum of the distinct values that occur exactly twice (0 if none).

examples.explanation: Values 2 and 3 each appear twice, so the sum is 2 + 3 = 5.
No value repeats, so the sum is 0.

constraints: Each value appears at most twice

title: Absent Values Count
description: `nums` has length `n` and each element lies in `[1, n]`, repeats allowed. Return how many integers in `[1, n]` do not appear in `nums`.

examples.explanation: Values 5 and 6 never appear among 1..8, so 2 are absent.
The value 2 never appears, so 1 is absent.

title: Corrupted Set Code
description: `nums` started as a permutation of `1..n`, but one value was overwritten by a copy of another, so one value appears twice and one is missing. Return `duplicate * 100000 + missing`.

examples.explanation: Duplicate 2, missing 3, so 2 * 100000 + 3.
Duplicate 1, missing 2, so 1 * 100000 + 2.

constraints: Exactly one value repeats and exactly one value is missing

title: Smallest Safe Starting Value
description: Pick a positive integer `start`. Walking left to right, add each element of `nums` to a running total beginning at `start`. Return the smallest `start` for which the running total never drops below 1.

examples.explanation: Starting at 5 the totals are 2, 4, 1, 5, 7; starting at 4 the total reaches 0.
Starting at 1 the totals are 2 and 4.

title: Windows Meeting Average
description: Count the contiguous windows of exactly `k` elements of `nums` whose average is at least `threshold`.

examples.explanation: Windows [2,5,5], [5,5,5] and [5,5,8] have averages of at least 4.
Only the window [2,3] has an average of at least 2.

title: Highest Altitude Reached
description: A biker starts at altitude 0. `gain[i]` is the net altitude change between point `i` and point `i + 1`. Return the highest altitude reached at any point, including the start.

examples.explanation: Altitudes are 0, -5, -4, 1, 1, -6; the highest is 1.
Altitudes are 0, -4, -7, -9; the start 0 is highest.

title: Candy Leaders
description: `candies[i]` is the number of candies kid `i` has. Count the kids who would hold the greatest number of candies (ties count as greatest) after being given all `extra` candies.

examples.explanation: The maximum is 5; adding 3 lifts the kids with 2, 3, 5 and 3 to at least 5, but not the kid with 1.
With 10 extra every kid reaches the maximum.

title: Monotonic Array Test
description: Return `true` if `nums` is entirely non-decreasing or entirely non-increasing; otherwise return `false`.

examples.explanation: The array never decreases.
It rises then falls, so it is neither.

title: Sorted Squares Checksum
description: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Square every element, sort the squares ascending, and return `sum((i + 1) * sq[i])` over the sorted squares using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: Sorted squares are [1,4], so 1 + 8 = 9.

title: Merged Sorted Checksum
description: `a` and `b` are each sorted in non-decreasing order (either may be empty). Merge them into one sorted array and return `sum((i + 1) * merged[i])` using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: Merged is [5], checksum 5.

title: Rearrangeable Progression
description: Return `true` if the elements of `arr` can be reordered so that the difference between every two consecutive elements is the same constant; otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Reordered as 1,3,5 the step is 2.
No ordering of 1,2,4 has a constant step.

title: Summit Position
description: `arr` is a mountain: strictly increasing up to one peak, then strictly decreasing, with the peak neither first nor last. Return the index of the peak in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The peak 5 sits at index 2.
The peak 9 sits at index 1.

title: Smaller Count Checksum
description: For each index `i`, let `c[i]` be the number of indices `j` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`. Return `sum((i + 1) * c[i])` using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: Counts are [0,0,0], checksum 0.

title: Equal Index Pairs
description: Count the pairs of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] == nums[j]`.

examples.explanation: The 1s give three pairs and the 3s give one pair, so 4.
All six index pairs of four equal values count.

title: Record High Count
description: Count the elements of `nums` that are strictly greater than every element before them. The first element always counts.

examples.explanation: Records are 3, 4 and 7.
Only the first 5 counts; equal values are not records.

title: Interleaved Halves Checksum
description: `nums` has length `2n` and is laid out as `[x1,...,xn,y1,...,yn]`. Rearrange it to `[x1,y1,x2,y2,...,xn,yn]` and return `sum((i + 1) * result[i])` using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: The result is [1,2], so 1 + 4 = 5.

title: Self-Indexed Permutation Checksum
description: `nums` is a permutation of `0..n-1`. Build `ans` where `ans[i] = nums[nums[i]]` and return `sum((i + 1) * ans[i])` using 0-based `i`.

title: Is Rotation Of Other
description: Return `true` if `b` can be obtained by rotating `a` some number of positions (including zero) to the left; the arrays must have the same length. Otherwise return `false`.

examples.explanation: Rotating [1,2,3,4] left by 2 gives [3,4,1,2].
Same length but no rotation matches.

title: Pairs Under Limit Count
description: Count the pairs of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] < target`.

examples.explanation: The pairs with sum below 2 are (-1,1), (-1,2) and (-1,1) using the last 1.
Every pair of 3s sums to 6, which is not below 6.

title: Merged Interval Count
description: `intervals` is a flat list `[s1,e1,s2,e2,...]` of closed intervals. Two intervals that share at least one point are merged into one. Return how many intervals remain after all merging.

examples.explanation: [1,4] and [4,5] touch at 4 and merge.

title: Clashing Interval Pairs
description: `intervals` is a flat list `[s1,e1,s2,e2,...]` of closed intervals. Count the index pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` whose intervals share at least one point.

examples.explanation: Pairs (0,1) and (1,2) clash; (0,2) does not.
The two intervals touch at 4, so they clash.

title: Missing Range Count
description: `nums` holds distinct integers sorted ascending, all within `[lo, hi]`. A missing range is a maximal run of consecutive integers in `[lo, hi]` that are absent from `nums`. Return the number of missing ranges.

examples.explanation: The missing ranges are 2, 4..49, 51..74 and 76..99.
Every integer in 1..3 is present, so there are none.

constraints: `nums` is strictly increasing and every value lies in [lo, hi]

title: Consecutive Run Groups
description: `nums` holds distinct integers sorted ascending. Group the values into maximal runs where each value is exactly one more than the previous. Return the number of runs (0 for an empty array).

examples.explanation: Runs are 0..2, 4..5 and 7.
The single value forms one run.

title: Fixable With One Swap
description: Return `true` if `nums` is already non-decreasing or can be made non-decreasing by swapping exactly one pair of elements (at different positions); otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Swapping the 3 and the 2 sorts the array.
Three positions are out of place, so one swap cannot fix it.

title: Hills And Valleys
description: A plateau of equal adjacent values counts as a single position. A position is a hill if the nearest different neighbours on both sides are smaller, and a valley if both are larger. Return the total number of hills and valleys in `nums`.

examples.explanation: 4 is a hill, the plateau of 1s is a valley and 6 is a hill.
The plateau of 3s has smaller neighbours on both sides, so it is one hill.

title: Lucky Value Lookup
description: A value is lucky when its frequency in `arr` equals the value itself. Return the largest lucky value, or -1 if there is none.

examples.explanation: 2 appears twice and 3 appears three times; the largest lucky value is 3.
No value matches its frequency.

title: Alternating Parity Stretch
description: Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray of `nums` in which every pair of adjacent elements has different parity (one even, one odd).

examples.explanation: The stretch 1,2,3,4 alternates for length 4.
Equal-parity neighbours break every stretch, so the answer is 1.

title: Zero Doubling Checksum
description: Duplicate every zero in `arr` in place, shifting later elements right and discarding whatever falls beyond the original length. Return `sum((i + 1) * arr[i])` of the final array using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: The array becomes [1,2,3], unchanged.

title: Odd Length Subarray Total
description: Return the sum of the elements of every contiguous subarray of `arr` whose length is odd, counting each subarray separately.

examples.explanation: Length 1 sums to 15, length 3 to 28 and length 5 to 15, giving 58.
Subarrays [10] and [11] sum to 21.

title: Reference Order Sort Checksum
description: Reorder `arr` so values listed in `ref` come first in the order they appear in `ref` (all copies together), followed by the remaining values in ascending order. Return `sum((i + 1) * result[i])` using 0-based `i`.

examples.explanation: No value of `ref` appears, so `arr` is simply sorted to [1,2,3].

title: Seat Assignment Moves
description: `seats[i]` and `students[i]` are positions on a line; both arrays have the same length and no seat is shared. Each move shifts one student by 1. Return the minimum total moves so that every student sits in a distinct seat.

examples.explanation: Sorted seats 1,3,5 and students 2,4,7 need 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 moves.
Sorted seats 1,4,5,9 and students 1,2,3,6 need 0 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 moves.

title: Truck Loading Units
description: `boxes` is a flat list `[count1,units1,count2,units2,...]`: box type `i` has `count_i` boxes each worth `units_i`. A truck holds at most `truckSize` boxes. Return the maximum total units it can carry.

examples.explanation: Take 1 box of 3 units, 2 of 2 units and 1 of 1 unit: 3 + 4 + 1 = 8.
The truck carries 3 of the 5 boxes at 10 units each.

title: Farthest From Occupied Seat
description: `seats[i]` is 1 if seat `i` is occupied and 0 if empty, with at least one of each. Choosing an empty seat to maximise the distance to the nearest occupied seat, return that maximum distance.

examples.explanation: Seat 2 is two away from both neighbours.
Sitting in seat 3 is 3 away from the person in seat 0.

constraints: At least one seat is occupied and at least one is empty

title: Heaviest Ascending Stretch
description: Return the largest sum over all contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose elements are strictly increasing. A single element counts as an ascending subarray.

examples.explanation: The stretch 5,10,50 sums to 65, beating 10,20,30 at 60.
The stretch 10,11,12 sums to 33.

title: Duplicate Via Value Chain
description: `nums` has `n + 1` integers, each in `[1, n]`, and exactly one value occurs more than once (possibly many times). Return that value without modifying `nums`, using O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: The value 2 appears twice.
Only the value 1 can appear, so it is repeated.

title: Best Sum With Minimum Length
description: Return the largest sum of a contiguous subarray of `nums` that contains at least `k` elements.

examples.explanation: The subarray [-3,4,-1,2] has 4 elements and sums to 2, but [4,-1,2,1] sums to 6 and is longer than 2.
With k = 3 the whole array [-2,-1,-3] is forced.

title: Largest Absolute Subarray Sum
description: The absolute sum of a subarray is the absolute value of its element sum. Return the largest absolute sum over all contiguous subarrays of `nums` (the empty subarray counts, giving 0).

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,-5,1,-4,3,-2] has sum -5... the best is [-5,1,-4] with sum -8 in absolute value 8.
All elements are positive, so the whole array sums to 6.

title: Unique Stretch Best Sum
description: Pick a contiguous subarray of `nums` in which all elements are distinct. Return the largest possible sum of such a subarray.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,4,5,6] has distinct values and sums to 17.
No two neighbours are equal across a distinct run, so the best is [5,2,1,2]? no: the best distinct run is [1,2,5] = 8.

title: Multiple-Sum Subarray Exists
description: Return `true` if `nums` has a contiguous subarray with at least two elements whose sum is a multiple of `k` (zero counts as a multiple); otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,4] sums to 6, a multiple of 6.
No subarray of two or more elements sums to a multiple of 13.

title: Sum Of Over-Third Values
description: Return the sum of the distinct values that occur strictly more than `nums.length / 3` times in `nums` (real division), or 0 if there are none.

examples.explanation: Both 1 and 2 occur more than 6/3 = 2 times, so the sum is 3.
Each value occurs once, which is not more than 3/3.

title: Earliest Same-Dominant Split
description: An element is dominant in an array if it occurs more than half as many times as the length, i.e. `2 * count > length`. Return the smallest index `i` (0 <= i < n - 1) such that `nums[0..i]` and `nums[i+1..n-1]` each have a dominant element and it is the same value in both; return -1 if no split works.

examples.explanation: Splitting after index 2 gives [1,2,2,2] and [2], both dominated by 2.
No value dominates both sides of any split.

title: Kth Absent Positive
description: `arr` is strictly increasing and holds positive integers. Counting positive integers that are absent from `arr` in increasing order, return the `k`-th absent one.

examples.explanation: The absent values are 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, ... and the 5th is 9.
The absent values are 5, 6, ... so the 2nd is 6.

title: Swaps To Sort A Permutation
description: `nums` is a permutation of `0..n-1`. In one move you may swap any two elements (not necessarily adjacent). Return the minimum number of moves needed to sort `nums` ascending.

examples.explanation: The cycles have lengths 3 and 2, needing 2 + 1 swaps.
The array is already sorted.

title: Increasing Triplet Exists
description: Return `true` if there exist indices `i < j < k` with `nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]`, otherwise `false`. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: The values 1 < 2 < 6 form an increasing triplet.
The array is strictly decreasing, so no triplet exists.

title: Shortest Removal For Divisible Sum
description: Remove a contiguous subarray (possibly empty, but not the whole array) from `nums` so that the sum of the remaining elements is divisible by `p`. Return the minimum length of the removed subarray, or -1 if impossible.

examples.explanation: The total is 10; removing [4] leaves 6, which is divisible by 6.
The total is 16; removing [5,2] leaves 9, which is divisible by 9.

title: Longest Ones After One Deletion
description: You must delete exactly one element from the binary array `nums`. Return the length of the longest subarray consisting only of 1s in the resulting array (0 if there is none).

examples.explanation: Deleting the 0 joins the ones into a run of 3.
A deletion is forced, leaving a run of 2.

title: Best Rotation Weighted Sum
description: Rotating `nums` right by `k` positions gives `B` with `B[i] = nums[(i - k) mod n]`. Return the maximum of `sum(i * B[i])` over all rotations `k` in `[0, n - 1]`.

examples.explanation: Rotating right by 3 gives [3,2,6,4] with weighted sum 26.
The single element sits at index 0, so the sum is 0.

title: Cells Covered Exactly K Times
description: `ranges` is a flat list of inclusive integer ranges: range `t` is `[ranges[2t], ranges[2t+1]]`. Return how many integers are covered by exactly `k` of the ranges.

examples.explanation: Only the integers 3 and 6 are covered by exactly two ranges.
The integers 1..3 and 5..7 are each covered once.

title: Intervals Not Covered By Others
description: `intervals` is a flat list of distinct closed intervals `[intervals[2t], intervals[2t+1]]`. Interval `[a,b]` is covered by `[c,d]` when `c <= a` and `b <= d`. Return how many intervals are not covered by any other interval.

examples.explanation: [3,6] lies inside [2,8]; the other two intervals are not covered.
[1,2] and [3,4] both lie inside [1,4].

title: Fewest Range Increments To Build
description: Starting from an array of zeros with the same length as `target`, one operation adds 1 to every element of any contiguous subarray. Return the minimum number of operations needed to obtain `target`.

examples.explanation: Three rises of 1 each need their own operation.
A rise of 3 at the start and a rise of 1 at the end give 4.

title: Make Values Unique By Increments
description: In one move you may increase any element of `nums` by 1. Return the minimum total number of moves so that all elements become pairwise distinct.

examples.explanation: Sorted 1,1,2,2,3,7 becomes 1,2,3,4,5,7 using 6 increments.
All values are already distinct.

title: Split Into Consecutive Groups
description: Return `true` if all values in `hand` can be arranged into groups of exactly `groupSize` consecutive integers (like 4,5,6), using every value exactly once; otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The groups [1,2,3], [2,3,4] and [6,7,8] use every card.
Five cards cannot be split into groups of 4.

title: Fewest Distinct After Removals
description: Remove exactly `k` elements from `nums`. Return the minimum possible number of distinct values remaining.

examples.explanation: Removing the 4 leaves only the value 5.
Remove 4, 2 and one 1, leaving the values 3 and 1.

title: Pair Up With Divisible Sums
description: `nums` has even length. Return `true` if its elements can be split into pairs so that the sum of each pair is divisible by `k`, otherwise `false`. Negative numbers use the mathematical remainder (e.g. -1 mod 5 = 4).

examples.explanation: Pairs (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), (4,6) and (5,10) all sum to multiples of 5.
Pairs (1,6), (2,5) and (3,4) all sum to 7.

title: Fewest Swaps To Align Row
description: Two rows `tops` and `bottoms` of equal length hold numbers 1..6 (a row of dominoes). One swap exchanges `tops[i]` and `bottoms[i]`. Return the minimum number of swaps after which all values in `tops` are equal or all values in `bottoms` are equal, or -1 if impossible.

examples.explanation: Swapping columns 1 and 3 makes the top row all 2s.
No value appears in every column, so it is impossible.

title: Token Play Maximum Score
description: You start with `power` and score 0. Each token in `tokens` may be used at most once: play it face up (costs `tokens[i]` power, needs `power >= tokens[i]`, gives +1 score) or face down (needs score >= 1, gives +`tokens[i]` power, -1 score). Return the maximum score you can reach at any moment.

examples.explanation: Play 100, trade that score for 400 power, then play 200 and 300 for a score of 2.
Power 50 cannot play the token and there is no score to trade.

title: Next Permutation Checksum
description: Rearrange `nums` into the next lexicographically greater ordering of its elements; if it is already the greatest, rearrange it into the smallest ordering. Return the checksum `sum((i + 1) * result[i])` over 0-based `i`.

title: Best Distinct Window Sum
description: Among all windows of exactly `k` consecutive elements of `nums` whose elements are pairwise distinct, return the largest window sum, or 0 if no such window exists.

title: Smallest Value In Rotated Duplicates
description: `nums` was sorted in non-decreasing order and then rotated by an unknown number of positions (possibly 0); duplicates are allowed. Return its minimum element.
constraints: nums is a rotation of a non-decreasing array

title: Arithmetic Subarray Count
description: Return the number of contiguous subarrays of `nums` that have at least 3 elements and whose consecutive differences are all equal.

title: Car Fleet Count
description: Cars drive toward `target` on a one-lane road; car `i` starts at `position[i]` with constant `speed[i]`. A car never passes the one ahead; it catches up and then drives at the slower speed, forming a fleet (meeting exactly at `target` also counts as one fleet). Return the number of fleets that arrive.

title: Widest Non-Decreasing Pair
description: Return the maximum value of `j - i` over all index pairs `i < j` with `nums[i] <= nums[j]`, or 0 if there is no such pair.

title: Days Until Warmer Checksum
description: For each day `i`, let `wait[i]` be the number of days until a strictly higher temperature appears in `temps` (0 if none ever does). Return `sum((i + 1) * wait[i])` over 0-based `i`.

title: Smallest Number After Removing Digits
description: Remove exactly `k` digits from the decimal string `num` so the resulting number is as small as possible. Return it as a string without leading zeros (return `"0"` if nothing but zeros, or nothing, remains).
constraints: num has digits only and no leading zero (unless it is "0")

title: Longest Index Cycle
description: `nums` is a permutation of `0..n-1`. Starting at index `i`, repeatedly jump to `nums[i]`, then to `nums[nums[i]]`, and so on until you would return to `i`. Return the largest number of distinct indices visited by any starting index.

title: Subarrays With Exact GCD
description: Return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose greatest common divisor equals `k`.

title: Subarrays With Small Score
description: The score of a subarray is its sum multiplied by its length. Given positive integers `nums`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays with score strictly less than `k`.

title: Best Sum With Length Multiple
description: Return the maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums` whose length is a multiple of `k`.

title: Best Sum After One Squaring
description: You must replace exactly one element `x` of `nums` by `x * x`. Return the maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray of the resulting array, over every choice of the replaced element.

title: Car Pool Capacity Check
description: `trips` is a flat list of triples `[passengers, from, to]`: that many passengers are picked up at position `from` and dropped at position `to` on a road driven in one direction. Passengers leaving at a position get out before new ones board there. Return `true` if the car never carries more than `capacity` passengers.

title: Longest Positive Product Subarray
description: Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray of `nums` whose product is strictly positive, or 0 if none exists.

title: Range Of Sorted Subarray Sums
description: List the sums of all non-empty contiguous subarrays of the positive array `nums`, sort them ascending, and return the sum of the entries at 1-based positions `left` through `right` inclusive, modulo `1000000007`.

title: Minimum Absolute Sum Difference
description: The absolute sum difference of equal-length arrays `a` and `b` is `sum(|a[i] - b[i]|)`. You may replace at most one element of `a` with any other element already in `a`. Return the minimum possible difference modulo `1000000007`.

title: Valid Splits By Sum
description: A split index `i` (0 <= i < n - 1) is valid if the sum of `nums[0..i]` is greater than or equal to the sum of `nums[i+1..n-1]`. Return the number of valid split indices.

examples.explanation: Splits after index 0 (10 vs 3) and index 1 (14 vs -1) are valid; the split after index 2 (6 vs 7) is not.
Splits after index 1 (5 vs 1) and index 2 (6 vs 0) are valid; after index 0 it is 2 vs 4.

title: Group Ones Around The Ring
description: `nums` is a circular binary array (the last element is adjacent to the first). In one move you swap the values at any two positions. Return the minimum number of moves needed so that all the 1s form one contiguous block, wrapping around the end allowed.

examples.explanation: Swapping the 0 at index 1 with the 1 at index 4 gives [1,1,1,0,0], so 1 move.
The 1s at both ends already touch around the ring.

title: Subarrays With Large Median
description: The median of a subarray is the element at index `(len - 1) / 2` (integer division) of its sorted copy, so for even lengths it is the smaller middle value. Return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose median is greater than or equal to `k`.

examples.explanation: Qualifying subarrays are [2], [3], [2,3] (median 2) and [1,2,3] (median 2).
Only [5] qualifies; [1] and [5,1] have median 1.

title: Fewest Changes To Be K-Increasing
description: Array `arr` is K-increasing if `arr[i - k] <= arr[i]` for every index `i` with `k <= i < n`. In one change you overwrite any element with any integer; return the minimum number of changes that make `arr` K-increasing.

examples.explanation: Keeping only the 1 and changing the other four elements makes the array non-decreasing.
Even-index values 4,5,6 and odd-index values 1,2,2 are already non-decreasing.

title: Total Subarray Spread
description: The spread of a subarray is its maximum minus its minimum. Return the sum of the spreads of all non-empty contiguous subarrays of `nums`, modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: The spreads are 0 for singles, 1 for [1,2] and [2,3], and 2 for [1,2,3], totalling 4.
The 15 subarray spreads add up to 59.

title: Shortest Span In Endless Repeat
description: Imagine `nums` repeated forever: `nums, nums, nums, ...`. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray of this infinite array whose sum equals `target`, or -1 if there is none.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,3] sums to 5 and no single element does.
Taking 3 from one copy and 1 from the next copy gives sum 4 with length 2.

title: Best Window Through Index
description: The score of a subarray `nums[i..j]` is `min(nums[i..j]) * (j - i + 1)`. Return the maximum score over subarrays that contain index `k` (that is, `i <= k <= j`).

examples.explanation: Indices 1..5 have minimum 3, giving 3 * 5 = 15.
Indices 0..4 have minimum 4, giving 4 * 5 = 20.

title: Cheapest Sorted Insertions
description: Starting from an empty list, insert the values of `nums` one by one. Inserting `x` costs the smaller of two counts: how many current elements are strictly less than `x`, and how many are strictly greater than `x`. Return the total cost modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Inserting 2 last costs min(1 smaller, 2 greater) = 1; the others cost 0.
Insertions of 6, 5 and 4 cost 0, 1 and 2.

title: Weighted Equalizing Cost
description: Changing `nums[i]` by one unit (up or down) costs `cost[i]`. Return the minimum total cost to make all elements of `nums` equal to the same integer.

examples.explanation: Making everything 2 costs 2*1 + 3*1 + 1*3 = 8.
All values already equal, so the cost is 0.

title: Tightest Range Over All Lists
description: `k` sorted lists are stored back to back: `sizes[i]` is the length of list `i`, and `vals` is the concatenation of all lists, each in non-decreasing order. Find the smallest range `[a, b]` that contains at least one value from every list; range `[a, b]` is smaller than `[c, d]` if `b - a < d - c`, or if the widths are equal and `a < c`. Return it as the string `"[a,b]"`.

examples.explanation: The lists contribute 4, 0 and 5, so the tightest range is [0,5].
Values 1 (first list) and 1 (second list) give the range [1,1].

title: Best Arrangement For Range Queries
description: `queries` is a flat list `[l1,r1,l2,r2,...]` of inclusive index ranges (possibly empty). You may rearrange `nums` in any order. The total of an arrangement is the sum, over all ranges, of the sum of elements inside that range. Return the maximum possible total modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Index coverage counts are 1,2,1,1,0; matching sorted counts 0,1,1,1,2 with 1..5 gives 19.
Coverage is 1,1 on the first two indices, so the two largest values 5 and 6 are placed there: 11.

constraints: queries has even length with at most 10^5 ranges, 0 <= l <= r < nums.length

title: Tiniest Interval Per Query Total
description: `intervals` is a flat list `[l1,r1,l2,r2,...]` of inclusive ranges; the size of `[l, r]` is `r - l + 1`. For each value `q` in `queries`, take the size of the smallest interval containing `q`, or -1 if none contains it. Return the sum of these answers (the -1 values included).

examples.explanation: The queries get sizes 3, 3, 1 and 4, summing to 11.
Answers are 2, -1, 4 and 6, summing to 11.

title: Skyline Corner Points
description: `buildings` is a flat list `[l1,r1,h1,l2,r2,h2,...]`; building `i` occupies `[l, r)` with height `h`. The skyline is the outline of the union of all buildings. List every point `(x, height)` where the skyline height changes (the height at `x` after the change), in increasing `x`, and return them as the string `"x:h,x:h,..."`; the skyline starts at height 0.

examples.explanation: Classic skyline: heights change at x = 2, 3, 7, 12, 15, 20 and 24.
The two buildings of height 3 touch at x = 2, so no change occurs there.

title: Alternating Weight Of K Disjoint Subarrays
description: Choose exactly `k` disjoint non-empty subarrays of `nums`, in left-to-right order with sums `s1, s2, ..., sk`; `k` is odd. The strength is `k*s1 - (k-1)*s2 + (k-2)*s3 - ... + sk` (weights `k, k-1, ..., 1` with alternating signs, starting positive). Return the maximum strength.

examples.explanation: With k = 1 the answer is the best single subarray, which is [-1].

constraints: 1 <= k <= nums.length, k is odd, nums.length * k <= 10^6

title: Fewest Changes For Equal Pair Sums
description: `nums` has even length `n`, and every value must stay within `[1, limit]`. In one change you replace any element with an integer from `[1, limit]`. Return the minimum number of changes so that `nums[i] + nums[n - 1 - i]` is the same for every `i` in `[0, n/2)`.

examples.explanation: Pair sums are 4 and 6, so one change equalizes them.
All three mirrored pairs already sum to 3.

title: Adjacent Swaps For K Consecutive Ones
description: In one move you swap two adjacent elements of the binary array `nums`. Return the minimum number of moves needed to obtain `k` consecutive 1s somewhere in the array (`k` never exceeds the number of 1s in `nums`).

examples.explanation: Moving the last 1 next to the one at index 3 takes one swap.
The leading 1 must cross five zeros to reach the final two 1s.

title: Fewest Deletions For Summit Shape
description: Delete as few elements of `nums` as possible so that what remains (order kept) is a mountain: length at least 3, strictly increasing up to a peak that is neither the first nor the last element, then strictly decreasing. Return the minimum number of deletions, or -1 if no mountain can be formed.

examples.explanation: Keep 1,5,6,3,1 and delete three elements.
No peak can sit strictly inside a length-3 increasing array.

title: Smallest Spread After Forced Shifts
description: You must change every element of `nums` exactly once, either to `nums[i] + k` or to `nums[i] - k`. Return the minimum possible value of (largest element - smallest element) after all changes.

examples.explanation: Shift 1 up, 3 up and 6 down to get 4, 6, 3 with spread 3.
Shift 0 up and 10 down to get 2 and 8.

title: Earliest Query To Zero Out
description: `queries` is a flat list `[l1,r1,l2,r2,...]` of inclusive ranges. Applying query `j` lets you choose any subset of indices in `[lj, rj]` and decrease each chosen element of `nums` by exactly 1. Return the smallest `k` such that, using only the first `k` queries, `nums` can be turned into all zeros (0 if it already is), or -1 if even all queries are not enough.

examples.explanation: After two queries indices 0 and 2 are each covered twice, enough to zero them.
Index 0 is covered only once but needs 4, so it is impossible.

constraints: queries has even length with at most 10^5 ranges, 0 <= l <= r < nums.length

title: Floor Quotient Pair Total
description: Return the sum of `floor(nums[i] / nums[j])` over every ordered pair of indices `(i, j)` (including `i == j`), modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Same-value pairs give 3, plus 2+4+1 from the larger-over-smaller pairs, totalling 10.
All 36 ordered pairs give 1.

title: Window Negative Rank Total
description: For every window of `k` consecutive elements, look at the `x`-th smallest value in it (counting from 1, equal values counted separately). If that value is negative, add it to the answer; otherwise add 0. Return the total over all windows.

examples.explanation: Window values -1, -2, -2 (the 2nd smallest) sum to -5.
The 2nd smallest of each window is -1, -2, -3, -4 (the larger one), sum -10.

title: Window Size Best Minimums
description: For each window size `w` from 1 to `n`, find the maximum, over all windows of `w` consecutive elements, of the window's minimum value. Return the sum of these `n` answers.

examples.explanation: Best minimums per window size are 70,30,20,10,10,10,10.
Best minimums per window size are 3, 2 and 1.

title: Subarrays Capped By Equal Ends
description: Count the non-empty contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose first element equals their last element and that value is also the maximum of the subarray. A single element counts.

examples.explanation: Five single elements plus the pair [3,3] give 6.
Three singles, two pairs and the full triple give 6.

title: Best Team Performance Score
description: Engineer `i` has speed `speed[i]` and efficiency `efficiency[i]`. Choose at most `k` engineers; the performance of a team is (sum of its speeds) * (minimum efficiency in the team). Return the maximum performance modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Engineers with speeds 10 and 5 and minimum efficiency 4 give 15 * 4 = 60.
Adding the speed-2 engineer gives 17 * 4 = 68.

title: Best Point Pair Value
description: `points` is a flat list `[x1,y1,x2,y2,...]` with strictly increasing `x`. For indices `i < j` with `xj - xi <= k`, the value of the pair is `yi + yj + |xi - xj|`. Return the maximum value over all valid pairs (at least one pair is valid).

examples.explanation: Points (1,3) and (2,0) give 3 + 0 + 1 = 4.
Only (0,0) and (3,0) are close enough: 0 + 0 + 3 = 3.

constraints: 1 <= k <= 4 * 10^8, and at least one pair has xj - xi <= k

title: Tasks Assignable With Boosters
description: Task `i` needs a worker with strength at least `tasks[i]`, and each worker takes at most one task. Up to `pills` different workers may each take one booster that adds `strength` to their strength. Return the maximum number of tasks that can be completed.

examples.explanation: Worker 0 takes the booster for task 1; the two 3s take tasks 3 and 2.
Only one booster exists, so only one task can be done.

title: Total Sorted Gap Imbalance
description: The imbalance of an array is the number of adjacent pairs in its sorted order whose difference is greater than 1. Return the sum of the imbalances of all contiguous subarrays of `nums`.

examples.explanation: [3,1], [3,1,4] and [1,4] each have imbalance 1.
Subarrays with 1 and 3 but no 5 give 3, with 3 and 5 but no 1 give 3, and the full array gives 2.
